title: Beyond Passenger Growth: Human Capital and Regional Resilience in Alberta Aviation
content: Aviation growth is an incomplete measure of strategic success when activity concentrates at large airports while service elsewhere contracts. This study examines that problem in Alberta through public secondary evidence and a reproducible strategic investment model. Using a frozen Statistics Canada release, we compare published provincial totals with Calgary and Edmonton airport activity. Between 2019 and 2025, Alberta’s enplaned and deplaned passenger events increased by 2.52%, while the residual outside the two airports decreased by 31.80%; reported passenger flights in that residual decreased by 45.07%. These descriptive differences do not identify their causes or measure route-level accessibility. We then formulate a finitescenario portfolio model in which service requires both physical and effective workforce capacity. Capital projects, workforce programmes, and a joint continuity programme compete for a common budget, subject to optional regional service floors. An illustrative six-role, five-scenario experiment evaluates all 8,192 portfolios. An exact feasibility characterization distinguishes a financial shortfall from a capability limit. Requiring 60% minimum regional coverage raises achieved minimum coverage from 52.27% to 62.00%, while increasing maximum normalized regret from 4.16% to 7.65%. A tighter target eventually becomes technically infeasible, and additional stress tests expose limits to the scenario guarantee. The model is not calibrated to Alberta intervention effects. Its contribution is an auditable way to distinguish growth from distributed service, make human-capital complementarity explicit, and disclose the commercial trade-offs of regional commitments before investment decisions are made.
